title: Krishna Reveals His Divine Form
story:
The child in Vasudeva's arms was a newborn, small and new to the world. Then, in an instant, he was not only that.

Still lying where he had been born, the child took on a form no infant could take. Four arms, eyes like lotus petals, and in his hands the conch, the discus, the mace and the lotus. A crown of precious stone rested on his head, bright earrings hung from his ears, and his hair fell around him in a thousand shining locks. Vasudeva looked down and his eyes widened with wonder, for he understood at last whom he was holding. He bowed his head and folded his hands, and he began to praise the Lord he held as his own son.

He spoke of how the whole world arises from him and rests in him, and of the three colors he assumes, the white that preserves, the red that creates, the dark that brings an age to its end. He called him the one who creates and sustains and withdraws the three worlds by his own power, though he himself is never touched by the qualities he sets in motion. He spoke of how the child could not be known through the senses but only through the discerning mind, and of how he had come down into his own house to protect the world. Then his praise turned to fear. The cruel Kamsa, he said, had already killed every child born before this one, and even now, hearing of this birth, he would be coming with weapons in his hands.

Devaki too looked on the child and knew him. She praised him as the light that cannot be seen, the changeless one behind all change, the witness whom no name and no form can hold, the lamp that lights the soul itself, and she took refuge in him as the abode of peace, the one who stills the fear of all who are afraid. But her fear was sharper than her husband's. May that wicked one never learn of your birth, she said. Save us from the terrible son of Ugrasena. Hide this extraordinary form, O soul of the universe, before he finds us.

Then the child answered them. He spoke of a time long before this life, when the two of them had been a childless couple, set by Brahma to bring forth children into the world. They had turned away from every worldly pleasure, and through rain and wind and heat and cold they had performed long and terrible austerities, living on fallen leaves and air, their minds held still, and at the end of it he had appeared to them and offered them a boon. And they had asked, seeing no one else in the world who could equal him in character and in generosity, for a son like himself. He had granted it.

Then he told them the rest. He had been born to them once in that first life, and again, later, as the son of Aditi born of Kashyapa. Now, in this third birth, he had come to them again with the same form, and he had shown it to them now, he said, so that they would remember: their long penance, the boon, and the many times they had known him both as child and as Lord.

You have known me, he told them, as your son and as the divine, again and again.

Then, having spoken, the Lord withdrew the dazzling form. The four arms were gone, the crown and the earrings and the thousand locks. In Vasudeva's arms there lay an ordinary infant again, quiet and small. And the parents held him, and understood that the child they had been given was also the one who had chosen them, not once, but three times.
reflection: The Lord's words do the work that the splendor only begins: he reminds his parents that their son is also their Lord, and that their love for him is not new but very old. What looks like a miracle of light resolves into a quieter truth, remembrance.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana (5.3) folds this revelation into the moment of the birth itself; the Bhagavata Purana tells it as the child's own speech to his parents.
next_story_tease: But the child could not stay in the prison; before dawn, Vasudeva would have to carry him across the river.
hero_scene: The newborn Krishna revealing a four-armed form, conch, discus, mace and lotus in his hands, crowned and radiant, as Vasudeva and Devaki bow before him in the prison cell.
